Got it. That's a helpful elaboration, Jay. Then perhaps following up on that idea of de-risking more of the position, it looks to me, I'm not looking at any kind of contours or anything, but it looks to me that if you look at the wells you've drilled and the permits that you have, it's mostly along that what looks like that kinda southwest-northeast strike axis. I wonder, is that in fact the case? If it is, when or what's the right time to push it, push the de-risking kind of in a northwesterly, up dip direction?
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
When we started five years ago, you have a blank sheet of paper, like you're in kindergarten, you got a sheet of paper, there's nothing on it. All of a sudden we look and say, maybe we should drill this Circle M well. Now all that acreage that you see that we present, we didn't own any of that. We said, okay, let's drill the Circle M well. As you progress, it's almost quarter by quarter, year by year, we're able to buy the big position from Legacy Reserves, which had Pinnacle. We didn't know if the Pinnacle plant in that 145 mile high-pressure pipeline whether it was located at the right spot.
We did know that the logs that we had showed that on the, there was a boundary kind of on the east side. We did with our hundreds of landmen, we did find out that that was unleased. You go and you aggressively, yet prudently, grab what is unleased, and then if you can add HBP acreage, which most of that is to the west. 80%+ of our acreage is HBP, but we didn't add that HBP acreage. It was March of last year, we added 185,000 net acres. It was probably Q1, we added another 62,000 net acres. The acreage that you're seeing to the west, most of that's HBP.
We've said over and over, we've got to drill about 70 wells to hold acreage that we leased in this 520,000 net acre play. We have focused our most part of drilling to hold acreage, and then we'll deviate over and drill some of the HBP acreage. Now we will. We've had one pilot well core, and we've got a second one that we're working on right now. As we go through 2025, 2026, we would like to have a core of our own on all four corners of the footprint and a few in the middle. That will tell you the answer to the question that Derrick asked what is the rock quality? We're gonna know that with the cores.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
That is helpful detail. Thank you, Jay.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yes, sir. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Jacob Roberts from TPH & Company. Please go ahead.
Jacob Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Good morning.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Jacob Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Maybe a bit of a macro question, but if we see gas prices cooperate through the end of the decade, how many rigs do you envision the Western Haynesville being able to support over that timeframe? Maybe as a sidecar to that, is there an internal view to take a more methodological approach to growth and target high single digits or low double digits through the end of the decade?
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
I think, if you have all of this except like 6,000 acres is undedicated. I think you have to look at that and say, we're gonna probably connect 15 or 20 new wells to sales. Then as Dan mentioned earlier, when Derrick or maybe Kalei asked the question of how many more wells you're gonna drill around Elijah 1. Fortunately, we have an incredible partner in Pinnacle with Quantum, so we do control a budget for our gathering. Then the other question was asked, how about AI? How about the data centers, et cetera?
Now I think if we'll be able to control it, we will never have to drill a well that we shouldn't be drilling. We'll never oversupply the market because, of course, you have to drill wells. I think you will see us very prudently develop this and de-risk all four corners in the middle of it with the Pinnacle Gas Services, which makes our wells far more economic. I think that'll serve data centers. I think you're gonna see, we're 100 miles away from Dallas, 100 miles away from Houston. We're where you should have a data center.
I think with BKV and the carbon capture, we're gonna be far more attractive for companies that will look to approach us, and we're already in discussions with them to create the data center. Which goes back to this power demand. I think we're gonna be able to fulfill our share of the power demand. You look and you say, is it real? You always say, where's Waldo? Is this real? Do you really need this gas? We know we looked in the world's largest electric utility this week said that US power demand will probably grow by 450 GW. That's 71 Bcf of gas, which is what?
That's 75 GW with gas-fired. That's 12 Bcf of new gas that's needed. You got Woodside Energy's announced they probably have two Bcf by 2029 or 2030. Current permitted LNG projects are about 17 Bcf. This is a great question. Where are you gonna get that gas? We think that Appalachians could strain. You'll get a Bcf or so. Gotta thank the Permian. You don't drill there for gas. This is the core area why we worked really hard and fought hard to de-risk this stuff, to deliver it to you, when we need to.
That's. We're always going to protect the balance sheet, but we're going to de-risk this thing and take risk to de-risk it just like the Elijah 1.
Jacob Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Great. I appreciate the answer. The second question, kind of circling back to Freestone and some of the comments y'all made about timing it perhaps with the midstream build-out as we progress into Q4, into 2026. Is there anything we should be thinking about on the Elijah 1, in terms of flow rate versus the IP rate? Or if that dynamic will apply to any other wells planned for this year?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
The flow rate on the Elijah 1 is, we're flowing it basically the same type curves that we've got set up for all the wells back to the core. I don't think anything on the midstream side is gonna constrain us on, the ability to flow them how we want to flow them. We just need to be able to get the midstream in place to be able to drill these, which is why we don't. It's why we're not spudding another well up there until the end of this year and really mostly into next year. No, the well looks as good as everything else we have.
We're gonna flow it the same as the other wells we have. We don't have any constraints on the midstream side.
Jacob Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Excellent. Appreciate the time.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you. Great questions.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Carlos Escalante from Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Good morning, gentlemen. Thank you for taking my question.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Morning. Considering that 2025 is an HBP-driven program, so to speak, if I jump forward to 2026, what is y'all's underlying assumption for that year's program in terms of capital allocation in between HBP exclusive wells versus delineator/appraisal wells? To conclude the question, it would be tremendously helpful to understand and parse out the general geography of where these HBP wells are and their underlying impact to the perception of those well results as we move through the next 24 months.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. We still want to focus on when we drill a well in the Western Haynesville into holding acreage. Remember, we have that 70 wells or so that to hold this acreage that we leased versus the acreage we acquired that's held by the shallow production. That will always be a big priority, over anything else. Yeah. That and just the proximity and availability of midstream and acreage are for the next 25, 26 to both be similar. Those will be the main drivers to where they'd drill these wells.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Yeah. Thank you, Roland. I maybe should have clarified that I was asking specifically about the Western Haynesville, not to the entirety of the Haynesville.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
That is the Western Haynesville, right.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Yes.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. Obviously, legacy Haynesville, we don't have any acreage to drill the hole, but so that's very, price driven and, yeah, and takeaway is there are areas that the takeaway is more difficult in the legacy Haynesville. There are different costs to the transport in the legacy Haynesville, so we take that into account. Generally, we fill in the legacy Haynesville locations.
Since we haven't been that active there, we're actually able to go back into some of our higher performing areas with the rig we just added and drill with the legacy Haynesville around that since we've created a lot of space by letting production kind of fall in that area.
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Yeah. Thank you, Roland. Appreciate it. My second question is turning to the macro real quick, and perhaps using one of the prior questions as a segue. Would you be concerned at all, if permitting around the Permian, even though you rightly point out, Jay, those wells are drilled for the oil, but unfortunately have a ton of associated gas. Simply they don't have the necessary takeaway capacity to the necessary demand center.
Would you all be concerned or what do you view that Permian gas if there was an outlet for that gas, from additional permitting, at the government level that would take more of that molecule towards the Gulf Coast or the general demand area? Is that something that you're thinking about or concerned about at all?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
I think that's all expected as far as the, obviously the Permian gas supply has to grow in order to fuel the big demand pool that's coming from LNG and other power generation. That, yeah, that's gonna be a big contributor. We do think that the weak oil prices today kind of stall a lot of the interest in drilling those wells since they are drilled mainly for oil prices.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. Where would you expect that growth?
Carlos Escalante
VP, Wolfe Research
Thank you, gentlemen.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Phillips Johnston from Capital One. Please go ahead.
Phillips Johnston
Analyst, Capital One
Thanks and congrats. Wanted to ask about the quarterly shape of your TILs and just assess your confidence in achieving the large ramp-up in production in the H2 of the year that your midpoint of the guidance implies. It looks like you brought on 11 TILs in Q1 and are planning 12 to 14 or so in Q2. Combined for the H1, that's about half the 46 wells or so for the year. The TILs cadence seems fairly ratable by quarter. I'm just trying to reconcile that with the fairly flat production level in the H1 and then the large ramp-up in the H2.
Is that mainly a function of the timing of when those 12 to 14 TILs occur here in Q2? Is it a larger mix of Western Haynesville TILs in the H2 or some a combination of those factors?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
It's a combination of both. The problem that TIL related production models have is there's no way to know the timing of when those are brought on. The TILs in Q2 look to be more H2 weighted. That's why the production's really starting to see the production, the sequential production growth return in both Q3 and Q4. It's just a function of the types of wells that we're drilling and that we are completing at which time.
The Q3 and Q4, like you said, will be a similar amount of total TILs as the H1, but the profile would look pretty similar to the Q1 and Q2, where the Q3 will be a lower number of TILs and the Q4 will be a higher number of TILs.
Phillips Johnston
Analyst, Capital One
Okay. Perfect. Thanks.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
When they come on during the quarter.
Phillips Johnston
Analyst, Capital One
Yeah. Okay. Appreciate that. Obviously it's pretty early days regarding the BKV agreement. I'm sure a lot of details need to be hammered out, and there's tax credits to consider and whatnot. Looking out in the future, would you guys expect any incremental costs incurred by Comstock or any net capital outlays funded by Comstock?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
No. Yeah, our partnership is basically they will get the tax credits and they will make the capital outlays, and then we'll participate by receiving some. They'll purchase the CO2 from us. There will be a reduction in our operating cost net-net. Yeah, we don't see any big capital investment by Comstock.
Phillips Johnston
Analyst, Capital One
Excellent. Thanks, Roland.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Phillips.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Greta Drefke from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.
Greta Drefke
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Good morning, and thank you for taking my questions. My first one is on your lateral lengths. You've seen pretty consistently continued improvements across operations, particularly in the legacy Haynesville. How much further upside do you see the laterals on a sustainable basis? How would you characterize the applicability of these lateral lengths you realized in Q1 2025 going forward this year and into next?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
In the legacy Haynesville, yeah, we've gotten actually pretty long where we're at today. I don't see us getting a whole lot longer than this on average. We were at, what, just under 13,000 ft for Q1. Our longest one is 17,000 ft. We still have several 15,000 ft, 14,000 ft, 15,000 footers in our inventory. When you just look at the mix of what we're gonna be drilling as we go forward on the schedule, it's we're just getting pretty flat up there around that 12,000 ft to 13,000 ft average lateral length.
I don't think you're gonna see us continually, like, keep climbing higher than that.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
The positive is, though, we will not have to drill a lot of the very short laterals for reasons because of the U-turn and horseshoe wells are now kind of replacing those. Where we had those scattered in the drilling programs than even last year in the first part of the year, we had short laterals. Our averages should be a little bit better because we won't have the really short ones to weigh it down.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Right. In most of the horseshoe wells we'll be drilling, they're gonna be 9,500 foot, and we got a few of them gonna be a little bit longer than that. As far as just the average, I think is what you were asking about going in the future, I think we're probably getting close to a plateau point.
Greta Drefke
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Got it. I appreciate that color there. My second question is just on D&C costs. Do you think that there could be some meaningful pricing concessions on rigs or crews as we head towards 2026, just given the broader, more macro uncertainty, especially potentially also the implications from the oil macro more idiosyncratically?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think that's a really good question. I think the answer is, yes. Compared to, if you would ask that question on the last call, obviously we're more optimistic we'll see some price concessions just with what we're seeing with the oil strip and where the activity may be headed in the Permian. I think we'll see that across the board on all services, rigs, frac crews. You know what I mean? Obviously, we got some of our rigs are turned up.
I think we'll see it on a lot of the smaller services beyond rigs and frac crews, I think, where you'll probably get a more meaningful percentage drop in vendor costs there, and also hopefully on our pipe prices, depending on what happens with the tariffs.
Greta Drefke
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Got it. Appreciate it. Thank you.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question comes from Noel Parks from Tuohy Brothers Investment Research. Please go ahead.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Hi, good morning. Just have a couple. Looks like a pretty exciting quarter in terms of the Longhorn well and everything going on. I did want to ask about maybe just overall. It used to be that before the shale era, rock that was too tight was off the table. I'm just wondering, do you see there being plays now where formerly the thinking was, it's too deep and too hot, that now could be available to make a second wave in shale, given what you've demonstrated you've been able to do in areas that a lot of pretty much everyone dismissed as just not workable?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think we've obviously made some big inroads, and I think a lot of people are looking at what we're doing and what we've been able to achieve with the depths and the temperatures. I don't think there would have been a lot of takers on trying to have a commercial development with these conditions just not too long ago. I think with the price environment, where it's headed over the next two years and the LNG demand, I can certainly see some people looking a little bit deeper than what they would have just a year ago.
Noel Parks
Managing Director, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Right. When you were talking about also the great improvement you had in just the drilling time on the Western Haynesville, and you listed using more pads, the drill pipe, and but you also mentioned specifically casing design improvements and use of bottom hole assemblies. I just wonder if you could just talk a little bit more about some details on the influence of those?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
One thing I always kinda just preach around here is obviously consistency. We've had some great results and we obviously keep. We just wanna be very repeatable and predictable to be able to deliver that. Some of that then comes with time and practice. Practice just as you keep drilling wells, you keep getting better. The insulated drill pipe has basically shaved days off drilling the lateral.
Obviously, where we're deep and got a lot of high temperatures, our motors and MWD tools on bottom, obviously things don't perform well when you put a lot of heat on them. The insulated drill pipe cools those temperatures down a little bit. It makes our motors and our tools just last longer. You don't have to make as many trips when you're drilling the lateral, so that's how you shave off days there. Casing designs, we've just basically been able to streamline, downsize our sizes a little bit, and we just got a lot better at picking where our casing points are.
Bottom hole assemblies, just as we've drilled more wells and gotten more data on how the motors are performing, which motors perform better, and basically how to tweak the designs on the motors for the temperature, we've just delivered better runs with that.
Greta Drefke
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Great. Thanks, Dan .
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. We looked at geology 30 years ago and said we thought the rocks were there. When the Joneses came in, he said, I'd like to drill this Circle M well. I said, okay. You had to progress day to day, just like our relationship with you. You have to handicap people and say Tuohy does this, Comstock does that, et cetera, et cetera. You have to perform. You have to perform, and you have to get in the game. Once you get in the game, you gotta say, is that seismic real? Are those logs real? Is that core real? How do you frack these wells, and look at the performance.
Our in-house reservoir group, they have to look at how hard do you draw these wells down? This is a team sport of Comstock. You gotta have a big backer saying, I want to, I wanna own something big. You gotta have some breaks where you get this HBP acreage. You gotta know how much you have to spend in order to hold all that acreage. Like Roland said, we're gonna drill our 70 wells. You gotta have some people join the team for financing, like Quantum. You have to get the gathering, and you got all this stuff.
Once you get a little bit comfortable in one area, you gotta jump out 24 miles somewhere else, because it is a very hard-fought road. I don't think anybody when gas was at a 30-year low, except for COVID, was eager to jump in and drill the wells that we were drilling, which were some of the hardest in the world, when we drilled them last year. Nobody. We pushed the reset button on how to add inventory. We pursued exploration. That's what we did.
Greta Drefke
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Great. Thanks a lot.
Operator
Thank you. This concludes the Q&A session. I will now turn it back over to Jay Allison for final remarks.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
All right. Again, I wanna thank all of you that are still here listening. We respect your time. I want you to know that all 255 people here at Comstock, we relish and we're thankful for the incredible opportunity to unlock what we see as this tremendous wealth. We love the chance that everybody's given us. It was almost 7.5 years ago when Jerry Jones's family started supporting and investing in the company. Ultimately, they own 71% of the company, but they asked three questions at that time. This is 7.5 years ago. What does your drilling inventory look like?
If you drill a well, can you turn it to sales immediately? If LNG really materializes, can you use that natural gas as feedstock gas? Those same three questions is what we ask ourselves today over and over and over for this whole conference call. We've really, really come a long way in the seven and a half years. We want to thank you that are our equity owners, financial backers, and all the service companies we depend upon to create this value chain. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Our Western Haynesville is located several hundred miles from the Gulf Coast, where 100 billion plus of LNG facilities are located. Our location is why LNG companies, utilities, data centers, and industrial users are contacting us to be a future supplier.
To have substantial natural gas reserves near the proximity of the growing demand on the Gulf Coast will serve us well in the next decade. The golden age of natural gas is here, and we're on the leading edge of technology to unlock the value of the Western Haynesville. Today is the very first day we've shown the location of our 518,000 net Western Haynesville acres as we have closed the large acquisitions we have been working on and captured much of the leases that we wanted.
We also are providing specific well data on the first 18 wells as we now have a large enough sample size to evaluate the results. Now I'll open up this call with our standard introduction and disclaimer. If you would all go to slide one.
Welcome to the Comstock Resources Q4 2024 Financial and Operating Results Conference Call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly results presentation. There you'll find a presentation titled Q4 2024 Results.
I am Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer of Comstock. With me is Roland Burns, our President and Chief Financial Officer, Dan Harrison, our Chief Operating Officer, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations. Please refer to slide two in our presentation to note that our discussions today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws. While we believe the expectations in such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct.
Now, if you would go over to slide four or slide three, which is our 2024 accomplishments. On slide three, we highlight our major 2024 accomplishments. Most importantly, we successfully navigated last year's very low natural gas prices. Our realized gas price before hedging of $1.98 per Mcf in 2024 represented a 30-year low if you exclude the 2020 COVID year. We acted early in 2024 to significantly reduce our capital spending by releasing two operated rigs and one frac spread.
We also suspended our quarterly dividend to conserve cash flow. We increased our hedging program, which improved our 2024 realized gas price by 20%. It also safeguards our 2025 and 2026 drilling programs by targeting 50% of our expected production.
We shored up our balance sheet by adding $100.5 million to an equity private placement with our majority stockholder and enhanced our liquidity with a $400 million senior notes offering. During this year of low natural gas prices, we were also able to grow our Western Haynesville footprint. We more than doubled our acreage position to 518,000 net acres by acquiring 265,000 net acres at a cost of $401 per acre.
We made terrific progress proving up our Western Haynesville exploratory play. We successfully turned 11 wells to sales with an average IP rate of 38 million cu ft per day, and now have a total of 18 wells producing in the play. In Q4, we were able to significantly reduce our drilling and completion costs in the Western Haynesville compared to the 2022 level. The drilling cost per lateral foot in our new play are down 33%, and the completion costs per lateral foot are down 28%.
Overall, our 2024 drilling program delivered solid results and proved reserve growth despite the lower activity last year. We drilled 50 or 42.9 net wells, successfully operated Haynesville Bossier wells with a strong average IP rate of 26 million per day. Our 2024 drilling program replaced 107% of our 2024 production and drove 6% reserve growth with 899 Bcf of drilling-related reserve additions and achieved an overall finding cost of $1 per Mcfe.
Despite suspending our quarterly dividend, we still delivered the highest 2024 total shareholder return among public E&P companies trading on a major exchange. If you would flip over to page four, it's the Haynesville Shale footprint. Slide four is an overview, first time ever, of our acreage footprint position in the Haynesville Bossier Shale in East Texas and North Louisiana. Note that this map is to scale. It's not distorted.
We have 1,099,000 gross and 819,000 net acres that is prospective for commercial development of the Haynesville and Bossier Shales. On the left is our emerging Western Haynesville, and on the right is our legacy Haynesville area. Since the beginning, our leasing program in the Western Haynesville play in 2020, we have grown our acres position to 518,000 net acres.
We still have around 1,300 net locations to drill on our 301,000 net acres in the legacy Haynesville, which currently has 895 net producing wells. Our legacy Haynesville acreage is 48% developed for the Haynesville Shale and 8% developed for the Bossier Shale. In comparison, our Western Haynesville has only 18 net producing wells and is virtually undeveloped compared to our legacy Haynesville. We expect our Western Haynesville acreage to provide more inventory per acre versus the legacy Haynesville.
Given the higher pay thickness and pressures we encounter in the Western Haynesville, we expect the Western Haynesville to yield significantly more resource potential per section than our Legacy Haynesville. I will now turn it over to Roland to discuss the financial results reported today. Roland?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
All right. Thanks, Jay. On slide five, we cover our Q4 financial results. Our production in the Q4 averaged 1.35 Bcfe per day, which was 12% lower than the Q4 of 2023, reflecting our decision to drop two rigs early in 2024 and have that frack holiday that we had in the Q3. The only well we turned to sales in our Legacy Haynesville area in the quarter was our Horseshoe well that we discussed last quarter.
Oil and gas sales in the quarter declined 5% to $336 million due to the lower production level, which was partially offset by better natural gas prices. EBITDAX for the quarter was $252 million, and we generated $223 million of cash flow during the quarter. We reported adjusted net income of $46 million for Q4, or $0.16 per share. In Q4, we recognized a $52 million tax benefit related primarily to R&D credits and other credits, and also due to a reduction in the Louisiana state corporate tax rate.
A higher provision for depreciation, depletion, and amortization accounted for the loss before income taxes in the quarter. The higher amortization rate resulted from the decrease to our proved undeveloped reserves, which were determined under SEC rules, where you have to use the first of the month average price looking back for the previous 12 months. Of course, that price was very low in 2024. On slide six, we recap the annual 2024 financial results.
Production for the full year averaged 1.4 Bcf per day, which is very comparable to the production we had in 2023. Natural gas prices that we realized in 2024 fell by 7%, resulting in our oil and gas sales decreasing 7% to $1.3 billion. EBITDAX in 2024 totaled $850 million, and we generated $675 million of cash flow.
With weaker natural gas prices and the higher DD&A expense, we reported an adjusted net loss of $69 million in 2024 or 24 cents per share, compared to the $133 million net income we had in 2023. On slide seven, we further break down our natural gas price realizations in the quarter and for the previous quarters.
The quarterly NYMEX settlement price averaged $2.79 per Mcf in Q4, and the average Henry Hub spot price in the quarter averaged $2.42. 45% of our gas in Q4 were sold in the spot market, so the appropriate market price, reference price for our gas that quarter was $2.62.
Our realized gas price during Q4 averaged $2.32, reflecting a $0.30 differential for the quarter. We were 51% hedged in Q4, so that improved our realized gas price, our realized gas price to $2.70. We also had a $0.05 Uplift to our overall gas price realization from purchasing third-party gas to utilize our available transport.
On slide eight, we detail our natural gas hedge position that we have to protect cash flows in this year and in 2026. We have approximately 50% of our gas production hedged for this year at an average price of $3.48 or better. 22% is in price swaps and the remaining is in the form of costless collars with a floor of $3.50 and a ceiling of $3.80. For 2026, 59% of our hedge position is in collars with the same floor level of $3.50, but a higher ceiling price of $4.35.
Then the remaining 41% of our 26 hedge position are in gas price swaps, which average $3.51 per Mcf. On slide nine, we detail our operating cost per Mcfe and our EBITDAX margin. Our operating cost averaged $0.72 in Q4, which was $0.05 lower than the Q3 rate. Our EBITDAX margin improved to 73% in Q4 as compared to 67% in Q3.
Our production and ad valorem taxes were down $0.03 in the quarter, primarily reflecting the lower statutory severance tax rate we have in Louisiana, which went into effect in the middle of the year. Our lifting cost of the quarter increased $0.03, while our gathering costs were down $0.05 in the quarter.
Overall, our G&A costs were unchanged at $0.05 in Q4. On slide 10, we recap our spending on drilling and other development activity that we had in Q4 and for all of last year. We spent a total of $240 million on development activities in Q4, and we spent $902 million for the full year. In 2024, we drilled 32 or 25.8 net horizontal Haynesville wells and 18 or 17.1 net Bossier wells. We turned 48 wells or 42.9 net operated wells to sales, which had an average initial production rate of 26 million per day.
On slide eleven, we recap our proved reserves at the end of 2024, determined based on year-end NYMEX market prices, which have been adjusted for our differentials as compared to the much lower prices that we'd have to use for SEC purposes, and to determine DD&A in the financial statements. Using year-end NYMEX prices, we're able to grow our proved reserves by 6%, even though we had reduced overall drilling activity last year.
Our proved reserves totaled seven Tcfe. We added 899 Bcf of drilling additions, which replaced 170% of what we produced last year of 528 Bcfe. You know, at the end of this quarter, I think we'll have some more results. I want you. I mean, it's you. It's our banks, it's our analysts, it's our equity owners, it's our bondholders that believe in what we're doing. I want you to always know what we're doing. Our goal in 2025 is to materially de-risk the whole footprint and see what the thicknesses are.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You know, Charles, I'll add too.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Please.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
As you look up in our core acreage up there, you know, some of our best wells are in the areas that are not as thick, like up around, like, you know, the Elm Grove area. I, you know, as far as just speculating, you know, if it's something thinner or thicker on how it's gonna perform, I don't think there's any correlation there at all, really.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Yeah. Is it really more just, you know, gas fill porosity is the biggest determinant then?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. I mean, obviously more gas in place, right? Thicker rock, but.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Yeah.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yes, definitely that does not correlate to, you know, how prolific it'll be.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
We have meaningful.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Got it.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
-bottom hole pressure differences.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Yeah. Interesting. Then one follow-up. Jay, you touched on this also. I think, Dan, you touched on this. A lot of focus on these newest batch of wells, and rightfully so. You continue to watch these other older vintage wells, and I'm wondering if you can talk about what you've learned from them, whether about the right way to manage the pressure drawdown, you know, the landing zones within these formations or the right completion jobs. I know. You know, every day that ticks by, you add to the data pile from those older vintage wells. Can you just tell us what you've learned in that respect?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
I think, you know, we obviously have been really laser-focused on the cost, just getting the wells down and TD'd. The landing zones, I think, you know, a lot of these wells where we drill are in the, you know, relatively thicker, you know, part of the play. We haven't really, you know, got real specific on, you know, if the landing zone should be a little higher or a little lower.
We just wanted to get the wells down, you know, and basically just TD these things as fast as we could. As far as the drawdown and perf and, you know, we've been pretty conservative. You know, I think we'll probably tweak that a little bit in the future.
You know, these last few wells, we like to IP them, you know, pull them a little bit harder and get the wells clean, make sure they're getting clean before we get flow back off of them. Then, you know, pull the rates back and start them, you know, basically on the type curve rate and just basically, you know, let them go from there.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, Charles, some of these wells.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Thank you for that in detail.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Some of these wells we tube up, some we don't. That's a big cost variance too. We figure out what we need to do or not do, as we drill more of these wells.
Charles Meade
Equity Research Analyst, Johnson Rice
Got it. Thank you, Dan and Jay.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
The next question will come from Kalei Akamine with Bank of America. Your line is open.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, good morning, guys. Jay Roland. I think the update here is being received well, so I'm gonna keep it quick here. Any early thoughts on 2026 on maybe holding activity here at seven rigs? It seems like the industry is falling in a rhythm with demand, and that's a really good place to be.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Right. No, I think that's the key. You know, one thing we wanted to make sure is that we don't produce too much gas, especially in one region area. We've been, you know, looking at that. We think seven rigs was always a really good level for the company to kind of maintain. I think we dropped to five rigs. You can see the impact of that. That's really too low of an activity level, but it was needed to help balance the market. You know, we're gonna get very comfortable with seven. We're gonna focus on getting our balance sheet, you know, back to like it was in 2022.
That's our biggest goal, and I think 2026 will be a year that we'll have the level of production and good gas prices to get the balance sheet in perfect shape. I think, you know, 2025, you know, that level we're running now, you know, we won't add any debt, and we'll slowly pay some down. Next year, we'll be able to really reduce debt significantly.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Roland, as far as the year-end 2026 bogey, you think somewhere under 1.5x is where the balance sheet would end up?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, I think, of course, you'll see the leverage ratio improve rapidly as we can start to count the 2025 results and take off the results of last year we had the low gas prices, you know, but yeah, we definitely want to get it down as quickly as possible to the 1.5x leverage area. That's probably something that we achieve in 2026. But I think we'll be, you know, way in the very low 2x leverage numbers as we kind of work our way through 2025.
A lot will depend on, you know, how strong gas prices are and then how, you know, we do have to rebuild our production a little bit to kind of get that leverage ratio, you know, to its more optimal level.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, that's a really good point, though. I mean, we said this, but other than COVID, gas price last year was the lowest it's been in 30 years. If you look at that, and you look at us getting rid of two rigs, you look at us having a frac holiday, and then you look at us adding 265,000 net acres in the Western Haynesville, you can see that we really monitor our leverage and our balance sheet.
We do that even in a very difficult year. At the same time, instead of M&A, we said we'd like to see if we can't grow organically. Typically, that's what these companies used to do. Because of the Joneses, they kinda uncapped us.
We could go in and, you know, as we were one of the first several companies to de-risk and discover the core Haynesville, we just took the same group down to the Western Haynesville, knowing what we were looking for. It took five years for it to turn out the way it's turned out right now. It's still preliminary, but if we're right, these reserves will be, they'll be massive. Our footprint is massive, and we're in the exact right part of North America for all this demand, particularly for LNG. It's gonna be a really beautiful story.
Kalei Akamine
VP and Senior Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
That's right. It's exciting to watch. Jay Roland, I'll see you guys in a couple of weeks.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yep. We look forward to it.
Operator
Our next question will come from Bertrand Donnes with Truist. Your line is now open.
Bertrand Donnes
Energy Research Analyst, Truist Securities
Hey. Morning, team. I just want to follow up on that, on the M&A topic, not necessarily on the western side, but with higher gas prices, you'd think most of the private owners are probably thinking about, you know, potentially selling or, you know, maybe does that incentivize you to look more aggressively, or are those sellers seeing the strip move up and maybe they're already seeing a $5 price that they wanna see or something like that?
Then the second part of that would just be, on the oil side, most of these private equity shops normally ramp up production before a sale. Do you see that happening or that's not exactly how it would work on a gas side?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, it's hard to predict how, you know, what they're looking at. But obviously, I think there are still some private companies out in the Haynesville that, you know, have invested a lot of capital, and now that you're in a good gas price, you know, situation, their business plan is to, you know, sell that, kinda like the same with the oil, the private companies in the Permian.
But we do see a very low level of activity in the Haynesville, so we certainly haven't seen any type of effort to ramp up at all from the public or private operators. We've seen great discipline, you know, in the basin.
I think all the producers really wanna get very comfortable that, you know, that the gas is really needed. You know, we've seen very volatile gas prices. I think everybody's being very cautious to say, "We're not going to oversupply this market, and maybe we undersupply it because we're so cautious.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, you can even see Q1, you know, we give guidance down. We're not gonna overproduce, period. You know, that guidance is a result of dropping those rigs. You know, we're not adding the rigs in the Western Haynesville to increase production right now. We're adding those rigs 'cause that's the best place for us to drill because we need to drill more wells to HBP more of the footprint. That's why we're doing that even. We don't see any E&P company out there out of control on their production rates, none of them.
Bertrand Donnes
Energy Research Analyst, Truist Securities
That's great. I think the market is happy to see that. For my second question, you know, several of your peers have started talking about potentially locking in a percentage of their production to contracts, either data center or LNG, and it seems like most have fallen in a 10 to 20% of their volumes. Is that where you guys feel like you'd fall, or you potentially have a larger appetite? Maybe you lock up, you know, acreage dedication in the Western Haynesville or something like that, you know, to backfill a demand project. Thanks.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a good question. We would also wanna look at having a portfolio of purchasers for our gas and not putting, you know, all our eggs in one basket. But we see, yeah, both being a major supplier to several of the LNG shippers and potentially, you know, looking at some power generation projects to back too. But again, I think having a good balance of that activity 'cause, you know, their demand comes at different times of the year.
There are great, good opportunities for the gas producers now to start to directly, you know, lock up with the industrial users and the exporters. I think it's a good time for us to create, you know, good relationships where we can have more stable prices and also, you know that we've got good, you know, we balance out our production to what we know the market needs.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, particularly, you know, probably 90% of our Western Haynesville is completely undedicated. I mean, completely. It's free range out there. We can kinda do what we want to with it.
Bertrand Donnes
Energy Research Analyst, Truist Securities
All right. Just wanted to clarify, so an acreage dedication for a demand project, is that coming back or are we done with that?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I'm not sure that, you know, acreage dedication is probably, you know, out there. I mean, typically, that it kind of comes to back up, you know, large amount of infrastructure, you know, to make it, you know, for the infrastructure partner to be comfortable that, you know, they can get their capital out. Here, I think, you know, with the way we've structured things, we're gonna be able to own all that.
I think instead, we wanna kind of look out and say, "Hey, we wanna take of our portfolio of gas, both from the legacy and the Western Haynesville, and then we want to portion it out to, you know, these direct contracts as we feel comfortable that, you know, it's a good fit." Obviously, we're looking for the, you know, what's the best deal for Comstock. Who's gonna pay the higher premium?
They all have kind of different needs and. But it's a very exciting time to be developing a new play like the Western Haynesville. At the same time, you know, there is a lot of market development opportunities that our gas industry hasn't seen in a long time. It's a great combination of those two together.
Bertrand Donnes
Energy Research Analyst, Truist Securities
Certainly. Thank you.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You know, this is probably a good time to talk about too, the reason we were able to go look at the Western Haynesville is because the value of our core. You know, we don't want anyone to ever overlook that 301,000 net acres and net inventory with plenty of takeaway there. That gave us the ability to come look at the Western Haynesville. That, along with the operational technical skill that we had. The value of the legacy allowed us to do the Western Haynesville.
Bertrand Donnes
Energy Research Analyst, Truist Securities
Perfect. Thanks for the answers, guys.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Jake Roberts with TPH & Company. Your line's open.
Jake Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Morning.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Jake Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
You know, I hate to ask about 2026 plus, but thinking about the 4-3 rig split, as we kind of progress through 2025, is that a level that can meet any HBP needs, any MVC needs with Quantum, or are you contemplating a, you know, 5-2, a 5-3? Just wondering, you know, what are the commitments as we get into 2026, 2027 that we might need to be thinking about.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, the real positive the way we've structured things is that we don't even need to maintain that type of activity to kind of meet, you know, any MVCs or other requirements. We've been, you know, very conservative as you build something out, you know, not to get over-committed. I think it's a very comfortable level, you know, for the company. It's really gonna be like, what is the markets? You know, where's the gas really needed? I think we would adjust that, you know, based on kinda how we see these markets go out.
I think we're very comfortable with the activity level and being able to run 4 rigs in the Haynesville will keep us on track to HBP all of our acreage and easily meeting, you know, supporting, you know, the build-out of the midstream.
Jake Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Okay, perfect. Maybe just a quick follow-up. I appreciate some of the discussion about your understanding of the broader Western Haynesville acreage that you've disclosed. Can you just frame, you know, the amount of seismic, the amount of historical work that's been done on this land that helps you understand it, the way you do?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I'd say there's been a lot of 3D seismic shot across all of this acreage. Just a lot of different vintage data that's out there that can be bought that has been tremendously, you know, helpful in kind of planning out where we want to drill.
We've got some future wells that we're gonna be drilling some pilot holes on and getting, you know, drill them all the way through the section, through the bottom of the Haynesville for well control purposes and geosteering. We've also got some future coring and stuff we're gonna do as far as, you know, just doing some more sites, you know, and to get the performance properties on the rock.
Jake Roberts
Director, TPH & Company
Excellent. I'll echo the sentiment of appreciating the update, guys.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Gregg Brody with Bank of America. Your line is open.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, guys. Just as we think about midstream for next year, what type of capital should we pencil in? Then when do you think you will exhaust the midstream JV, and how do you think about funding it after that?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, it's a great question. This is a, you know, with building a new treating plant. This was a big capital investment that we started making in Q4 and, you know, through this H1 of the year. We're gonna have a lot of treating capacity that's gonna be available to us starting, you know, in Q2.
We continue to look at our volumes and then decide when we want to add additional trains, you know, to either a new plant or adding to our north or south plants. We also have some good partners nearby that we've secured additional capacity, you know, in order to not have to build everything. We feel really good about where that is.
I think that the build-out of the midstream has amazingly fit almost perfectly with our five-year plan for it so far, and so we've been really pleased, and I think our partner has been too. I think that eventually, you know, as the entity now has a lot of volumes and it's gonna have a really good year this year, it's gonna be able to maybe, you know, maybe put in its own credit structure there, so we can kind of get less expensive capital to kind of fund some of its build-out.
That's probably gonna be, you know, more later in the year after, you know, after it's up and running and generating a very strong EBITDA. We're very excited about what Pinnacle can become and the value it's gonna be adding.
I think you look down the road, it's gonna be a very, very big asset for the company. Our structure, you know, once we return that capital with a preferred return, you know, that will revert 70% back to the company, and then we can buy out the minority interest if we'd like in the future also.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. The goal was as we were acquiring all this acreage, we wanted to control the midstream. We trusted, you know, Quantum as a company in lending money and supporting plays like this. We really trusted them. We wanted to see if there was something that we were missing.
When Quantum came in, looked at the acreage, looked at the well results at that point, which have only gotten better, I mean, they said, "We're back here with $300 million." We wanted to make sure that we would control that and it wouldn't be sold to some third party, which would then control what we'd be doing in the Western Haynesville. We didn't wanna lose control of that, and Quantum became the perfect partner.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
It's fair to say that between Quantum's equity and a potential credit facility at the JV, that entity is self-funding for the next several years.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Right. We would see it hopefully transitioning in the next year. I mean, really, as you get through 2026, that's probably where it doesn't really need. It'll start to be totally self-funding. We also see maybe bringing in some of our nearby operators could also help accelerate that if we can land some of those as customers as we build the system out.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Great. Thanks for your time, guys.
Operator
Our next question will come from Noel Parks with Tuohy Brothers. Your line is now open.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of Energy Research, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Hi. Good morning. You know, just thinking about the drilling time improvements you've already been able to achieve, I just wondered, could you just talk a bit about maybe what assumptions you had going in in your earliest well, and whether there's anything different now that you're this far in, sort of like what you know, you talked about some of the things you've tweaked, but I'm just wondering, you know, kind of what was your starting point like when you were approaching the play?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You know, it's an interesting question because when we, you know, we looked at everything we had done in the legacy, you know, on our Legacy acreage in all of the years past, and kind of just one of the real general things, you know, we had seen was before we ever started in the Western Haynesville, you know, in general, in the core, you know, all the wells were being drilled twice as long, you know, say 5Ks to 10Ks. At the same time, they were getting twice as long, you know, they were being drilled in half the time. There were a couple of.
You know, there was a couple of old wells that had been drilled, old horizontals that had been drilled back in 2010 down here in the Western Haynesville that was kind of provided some of the earliest data to take a look at, you know, that we looked at. They had a lot of just a lot of mechanical issues, collapsed casing, and just, you know, really was pretty ugly.
You know, we just looked at how many days it took them to drill those wells, and those were essentially 5,000-ish type wells. If you just applied the same industry progression, you know, of twice as long and half the days, that's kind of what we targeted, you know, and it was around that 75 to 80 day timeframe. That's exactly where we landed.
You know, on average, if you take out that sidetrack we had on our second well, we landed at about 80 days starting out. The good thing is that, you know, there's a lot of running room. These wells are deeper and harder, and we just have so much more room to run down here to get better versus we did up in the core.
Well, our confidence level grew. You know, we were gonna drill to 16,00ft vertical, and then, as our confidence grew with well after well after well, we did go to 19,000ft. We wouldn't have done that had we not had more confidence in the 16,000ft vertical. You know, on anything you do, anywhere you drill, the longer.
If you can just, you know, wells are good and you can keep drilling additional wells and you can increase your activity, you know, it's the old practice makes perfect. The more you drill, the better you're gonna get. The more the industry drills, the better the industry gets. You know, that's, you know, that's what we're seeing.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of Energy Research, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Great. Thanks. You know, understandably, there's been so much attention to us seeing the map for the first time and the results from the newest slate of wells. I just wondered if you could just talk a little bit about gas macro. You know, looking at your hedges, I was just wondering, is there anything particular about the $3.50 mark as where your downside protection is that you've been gravitating toward? Also, if you had any thoughts about what things are going to look like or might look like as the LNG ramp up continues along?
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, you know, we look today, and I just looked. This is US LNG fleet hit a new record high of 16.47 Bcf. You know, we are very positive on natural gas in the latter part of 2025, 2026, even 2027. When we look at the Western Haynesville, not the legacy, I mean, we do need to drill the legacy, of course. It provides us a very dependable revenue stream. But what we want to do, we want to guarantee that we can drill all these wells that we need to drill in 2025, 2026, and still delever the balance sheet. Our big land grab and a lot of money we spent on that, it's over.
We'll spend a little bit as we do even in the core, cleaning it up all the time, where that'll be perpetual, but we don't see any big acreage out there, positions that we're chasing that we don't have. This is purely, it's a protection of the balance sheet to get us back to have a dividend. You know, if we could have a dividend in the latter part of 2026, great.
Early 2027, whatever. We want to delever the company now, drill these wells, stay true to the midstream partner with Quantum, and deliver this gas when it's needed. Now, the beauty of this is nobody tells us when to drill it, how to drill it, or. We control it ourselves.
It's something we bought, we control, and where it is is perfect. You could pick a map. If you would look at where our pipeline is, which we showed that, Roland went over it, we bought that, a lot of that pipeline in one of our acquisitions. It is the backbone of where our footprint is. You could not have a better location for that pipeline.
It's not there by mistake. 20 years ago, that was the core of the core of where they were drilling. That's why that pipeline was there. It just wasn't worth anything when we bought it. Somebody had to, you know, reinvigorate it and put some gas in it, and we're the only ones willing to do it. It has become a very valuable piece of the company.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, the replacement cost for 246mi of high-pressure pipeline and-
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Treating.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
A treating plant, it would be unbelievable to have to put all that in from scratch. I mean, you're talking about the amount of equity that's already there is pretty phenomenal, so.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of Energy Research, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Great. Thanks. That's really helpful insight. That's all for me.
Operator
This is all the time that we do have for questions. I would now like to turn the call back to Jay Allison for closing remarks.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
I wanna thank all of you. It's a much longer call than normal. It's almost an hour and a half. We knew it would go longer. We didn't wanna cut anybody off. You know, again, I wanna thank you. There's probably 250+ men and women who make up the Comstock team, and a lot of them listen to the call. I wanna thank all of you as well. I wanna thank our loyal banks. I mean, the banks have believed in us.
The bondholders have believed in us. The equity owners have believed in us. The analysts have believed in us. I wanna say again, especially thanks to Jerry Jones and his family, who are the backbone support to unlocking the Western Haynesville value. You know, I gave an old cowboy spirit. I'll give you another one. It says, "If you climb up on the saddle, you better be ready to ride." We at Comstock are ready, and you can take that to the bank. Thank you.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect

content.text:
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
The project will deliver 23% in cost savings or $8 million, significantly improving the economics and also providing some additional benefits, such as reducing our surface footprint and lowering the emissions from fewer wellbores. We expect the well performance from the horseshoe wells will match that of our regular 10,000-foot laterals. Once this technology becomes more de-risked, we can further increase the average lateral length in our inventory by converting short laterals into long laterals and further enhancing our efficiencies. I'll now hand the call back over to Jay to summarize our outlook.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Okay, Dan. Thank you, Roland. Thank you. You know, Dan, you're talking about the horseshoe wells. I'm thinking about the majority owner of the stock is, owns the Dallas Cowboys. Cowboys and horseshoes go together. Thank you for that report. Let's go to page 15. I direct you to Slide 15, where we summarize our outlook for 2024. As we stated in the last quarter, we really have taken a number of steps in response to the significantly low natural gas prices this year. During Q1, we announced we'd release two of our operated drilling rigs. We reduced our rig count to five rigs. We also released one of our frac spreads, reducing our frac spreads to two spreads. We no longer now have any long-term commitments for our pressure pumping services.
With those steps and our 2024 CapEx is expected to be down 34% to 41% from the 2023 level. We suspended our quarterly dividend. That saved about $140 million a year in dividend payments. In late March, our majority stakeholder, Jerry Jones, invested an additional $105 million into the company through an equity placement that the company had. Starting in late February, you know, we did add significantly to our hedge position starting in Q4 2024 and extending that through the year-end 2026. We're targeting a hedge level of 50% of our expected production level through those years.
In early April, we further enhanced our liquidity position with a $400 million senior notes offering, and we continued to maintain a very strong financial liquidity, which totaled just under $1.2 billion at the end of Q2. Our industry-leading lowest cost structure is an asset in the current low natural gas price environment, as our cost structure is substantially lower than the other public natural gas producers. We remain very, very focused on improving upon our Western Haynesville play and continuing to add to our extensive acreage position in this exciting play. Our Western Haynesville acreage position totals over 450,000 net acres to date.
We believe that we're building a great asset in the Western Haynesville that will be well-positioned to benefit from the substantial growth and demand for natural gas in our region that is on the horizon, driven by the growth in LNG exports that began to show up in H2 of next year. I'll now turn it over to Ron to provide specifics for the rest of the year. Ron?
Ron Mills
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Jay. On Slide 16, we provide some financial guidance for Q3 and the remainder of 2024. For Q3, we expect our D&C CapEx to range between $135 and $185 million, and our full year D&C guidance range on CapEx remains $750 to$ 850 million. The midstream capital outlook remains unchanged, and the leasing capital for Q3 and Q4 remains in the $2 to $5 million range. The full year moved up $5 to $10 million just due to actual Q2 leasing costs. LOE and GTC costs both for Q3 and Q4, and full year remain unchanged from prior levels.
On the production and ad valorem, the guidance range remains the same, which includes the impact of a lower severance tax rate in Louisiana basically being offset by a higher ad valorem rate. The DD&A rate, as mentioned by Roland earlier, is expected to be higher through the remainder of the year, due to the current low prices. Looking ahead, though, we would anticipate that to return to our more normal level, in the kind of price environment that we see in 2025. No other changes to our G&A or interest outlook that we provided in prior quarters, and we continue to anticipate deferring virtually 100% of our deferred taxes. With that, I'll turn the call over to the operator for Q&A.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. We ask that you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up to allow everyone the opportunity to participate. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Carlos Escalante of Wolfe Research.
