You know, you're asking about the drilling. If you look at our efficiencies, and Dan's right, I mean, some of the tools and the casing, we do use that in the core, but it's how you use it. What type of intermediate do you set? Do you tube the wells up? What type of completions do you have? What kind of drill pipe do you have? I mean, there's a lot of ingredients in the kitchen, and not everybody produces the same final product. So it can be very difficult if you're drilling your first 19,000-foot vertical and 10,000-foot lateral well to come in there and have the success that we've had when you've got a really good operations group, and it took them 85 days the first time. Well, now you're at 54 days.
A lot of that skill set, you have to spend a lot of money to perfect it. When you can perfect it, then you can lower those costs, and you create real wealth. You have to have the footprint to do that in. We captured a footprint at very low cost with most of it being held by production. That's the difference in this play.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Great. Thanks a lot.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Paul Diamond of Citi.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking my call. Just a quick one. Wanted to drill down on the opportunity set across these, the theoretical horseshoe wells. In your inventory, you got about, call it 16-odd% of, you know, below 5,000 foot. I'm just trying to understand how much of those, you know, given current expectations, you think you might be able to convert and where that would place them kind of in the, in the larger, production cadence or drilling cadence?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a really good question. You're right, we do have about 15% or 16% of our total inventory is, you know, the short laterals. We're actually currently working through that process right now of how many of those we think we can convert over to long laterals. I think the majority of them that we can, I don't really have a real, you know, fixed number I can probably give you today. I'd say the majority of them we're looking at moving over. You know, like I said, the only reason that we could not would just be because, I mean, obviously, you have to have two, you know, you have to have two of the 5,000 laterals kinda side by side, right, to have the horseshoe opportunity.
Some of our short sticks in our inventory, you know, you just got one stick, basically. Obviously, that wouldn't be a horseshoe candidate. You know, other than that, I think every, you know, if you got two of them side by side, every one of those is a horseshoe candidate. We're working through that process right now, seeing which one of those we can, you know, convert. They'll go in our long lateral bucket, which right now, you know, that's about 26% of our inventory. We'll significantly boost that up above, you know, 25-26% and, you know, that percentage in the short laterals will get a lot lower, which will be great.
I mean, that opens up a lot more wells that has really good economics that we can basically, you know, decide to put on our drill schedule. Or should we, you know, for some reason, for a leasehold reason or whatever, we kinda need to drill it, you know, it'll still fit in with the, you know, what we normally would be drilling with good economics.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. That actually kinda pertains to my follow-up. Assuming or under current assumptions you guys are working with, how would a horseshoe, you know, two 5,000-foot compare economically to an existing 10,000-foot?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yes, substantial. I don't have numbers in front of me, but yes, substantial, you know, rate of return, substantial improvement. I mean, you're gonna save $8 million, $4 million per basically off those 5K laterals. You know, it just drives all the key parameters significantly higher. Like I said, the cost. The cost to drill a straight 10K, to drill a horseshoe well is essentially the same. You know, I said a 1% to 2% premium, but I mean, that's within the plus or minus of any well we drill on kind of where our costs are gonna end up. You know, we look at the economics for a horseshoe well to be essentially the same as all of our other 10K laterals.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks, Roland.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Gregg Brody of Bank of America.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, good day. Good afternoon, guys. Thanks for all the update. As the credit guy, I've started to see these horseshoe wells pop up a few places, and I realize there's some data. There's been a number of them in other basins. I'm just curious, is there something that we should think about that is tricky about these, or it really is just drilling a lateral in a U-shape that seems like physics suggests we can do that now?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Right. You know, sometimes, the old saying, necessity is the mother of invention. I mean, you know, you drill a 90-degree turn to drill these laterals already, right? You know, you do the 90-degree turn, you're drilling the lateral. It's the same tools, it's the same motors that we run. You just make another turn, and you just stay with it until it goes all the way around 180 degrees. Now, I think, you know, until you kinda have to do it, you know, or, you know, you're looking at your inventory, talking about improvement. You know, a lot of people probably just kinda don't push to go there. Really the...
I mean, look, there is a little bit more risk to drilling a horseshoe well and you know, you gotta get casing around the curve. You have to get you know, when you're completing and pumping your perforating guns down and plugs you know, for all your frack stages you know, all those have to get pumped around the curve. I mean, but really, that's. I think the risk of that's pretty small. The industry kinda already has shown it in the Permian and I think the Eagle Ford for these other areas. You know, I think you just gotta prove it out, and you just basically gotta show people the results. I think you know, after you do more of them, it becomes a little bit more routine, and the risk is you know, greatly diminished.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, for example, on our first well, I mean, we're pretty close to TD in that well. Last night, I know we were-
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
We're probably within 500 foot of TD.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
We have had zero problems drilling the well.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's my point. First well, no problems. We're within 500 feet to TD in it.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
You were being asked earlier about how much potential of your locations could be converted. Should we think that it's just the ones that are in the up to 5,000 feet, or should we think also about the 5,000 to 8,500 feet that could be converted? Just trying to get.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, it really.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Just trying to get a sense of how much of that. You didn't quantify it. I know it's early days, but
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
I'm curious if you have a range that you would think about there?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, that's a really good question, and we've already kinda had some internal discussions about that. You know, can you take a 7,500-foot lateral and turn it into a 15K horseshoe? Now, we're not ready to kinda jump out there and do that yet. Look, the industry gets better with time. They get faster, they get longer, tools get better. If you have the demand for tools and the demand for certain services, in time, they show up, and they get developed, and they get refined. I think in time, I think, yes. I think that the industry will maybe go there. I mean, look, a 7,500-foot lateral has a lot better economics than a 5K, so the rush to start doing 15K horseshoes is not really gonna be there right now.
I do see, you know, and it's what your acreage, it's how it's laid out and what, you know, your options are. You know, I mean, you if you got two sections or three sections, you know, like we'll typically just drill a 15K straight lateral. We're not gonna do a bunch of 7,500-foot horseshoe 15K laterals. You know what I mean? That's. It's a very good question, and I think yes. I think in time in the future, I think there'll probably be some people that will probably try to push the horseshoe lengths a little bit further. The one, you know, they do have a little bit more torque and drag.
I mean, obviously, when you're pushing and pulling pipe around a 180-degree bend, it adds more drag, you know, push, you know, tripping in and out of the hole. You know, a 10,000-foot horseshoe well is kinda maybe more like the equivalent of a 15,000-foot straight lateral when you look at the drag going in and out of the hole, if that makes sense.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
That does. Just to come back to my credit roots, just a few follow-ups that you might get for some credit guys. I don't see you getting a... You're at 3.4 today. I think you're okay for next quarter to get into 3 to 5 or not going through the 3.5. Is that fair? If not, is it just a pretty easy amendment that you would get? Just as part of that, you know, I know the dividend was suspended this year. Just as you look out in the future, how do you think about that today?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, Greg. Of course, obviously, the gas prices are, you know, if we knew exactly what they were, we could answer the question exactly. That, you know, the gas prices and where they end up being will be a big driver in the EBITDA, which is the biggest part of that ratio. You know, it's also, kind of, remember, it's a kind of a full four-quarter calculation assessed in one quarter. Yeah, we stay pretty close to that level. We do think we can get a temporary waiver if we needed it, but we didn't need it, so, you know, we didn't go out and get it. So things kinda came in exactly as we thought they would.
We knew we were gonna get to that 3-4, luckily, we stayed there. We'll monitor it in Q3, you know, as hard as we monitored it in Q2.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Okay.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Then the dividend, obviously, I think we're, you know, we're not really talking about a dividend, you know, until we kinda get the leverage way down and, you know, looking off in the future. I think our first priority, you know, is to get back to generating good free cash flow, and then that will be used for some debt reduction to get the leverage ratio, you know, back to. We'd like to get back to levels that we were seeing, you know, back in 2022. You know, like we got to under, you know, closer to one times leverage.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, we were really monitoring Q2, and again, we did stay fine. In Q3, we didn't expect gas to be $1.90 on Monday. You do look at that price and say, Well, okay, so you gotta really monitor Q3. In Q4, you know, we would expect a little price appreciation and the hedges come in and help. After that, I think we're gonna have some big production growth. So that's it. We're kinda going through that valley right now. It's a good question.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
I appreciate the time, guys, and the education.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Thank you, Greg.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Geoff Jay of Daniel Energy Partners.
Geoff Jay
Partner, Daniel Energy Partners
Hey, guys. Just a real quick one for me. Earlier, you said you would expect to see D&C costs go down to something like normal levels. I guess I've kinda forgotten what normal looks like given all the inflation we've seen over the last year or so. Where do you kinda think those will trend given the service cost inflation that's out there and the efficiencies you're achieving?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, we think our legacy Haynesville, you know, main product, you know, will trend back to that, you know, a little bit below $1,500. That's $1,500. $1,400 to $1,500 is kind of an area, you know. I think, you know, the way we report this is kinda when wells are completed and they. You know, it's not really a good indication of where things are now because some of the wells we completed this quarter were actually drilled last year. Maybe we'll come back and add some additional information here and show you, here's the real drilling costs being incurred each quarter, and here's the completion costs being incurred.
They'll be on different wells, but they'd be more indicative of where costs are versus the process here of scoring is costs that were incurred in, you know, different periods than the one you're hearing about, so. Also, if you have a certain group of wells, you know, that are different and they're more costly, that happen to be the ones turned to sales, they dominate the numbers. As is the case this quarter, you have these Lake Bistineau wells that have a lot of. It's a high-cost area, period, and plus you throw some drilling problems in, and those wells kinda really distorted, you know, what would've been just looked pretty comparable to the other quarter if they weren't in there.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
We got less wells to average it down.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, we'll probably try to maybe provide some supplemental. You know, that will allow you to see the current cost of the quarter, how they're trending, you know, versus seeing something that occurred maybe, you know, even last year.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
Excellent. Well, thank you for that.
Operator
Thank you. I would now like to turn the conference back to Jay Allison for closing remarks. Sir.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
All right. Thank you again. We've gone over our hour, but as you know, the company, we've always had a vision. I think Greg asked about, you know, do you drill these horseshoe wells that are 7,500 foot to times two, 15,000 feet? The answer is, we have a vision, and we had a vision to step out 100 miles and see if we could rebirth a major gas play, which is now the Western Haynesville. We have a vision, and then we always monitor where gas supply is. If you look, we've been looking for the last probably six or seven weeks, and that gas storage level is about 38% above the five-year average. Well, week after week after week, that's come down. It's like 16% above the five-year average.
It's coming the right way, and we're coming into the three, four, five weeks of what we call the real meat of the summer. We do see that. We see LNG at over 13 Bs a day right now. It's back. Freeport is back. Then we look past September, October, and you see the startups of Corpus Christi Stage 3 in Plaquemines. We see a strong Q4 2024 run from the LNG fleet, and that goes into 2025. We're committed to sharing everything that we can share in all of our areas and to protect our balance sheet.
again, I wanna compliment the Joneses for, you know, writing the $100 million check for the acreage that we've been acquiring. I think that acreage is worth a fortune, and they were willing to backstop that and write the check. We're gonna be in good shape there. Thank you for your time. We appreciate it.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Operator
Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Comstock Resources, Inc. First Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press Star one one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press Star one one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer. Please go ahead.
Jay Allison
CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you. Welcome to the Comstock Resources Q1 2024 Financial and Operating Results Conference Call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly results presentation. There you'll find a presentation entitled Q1 2024 Results. I'm Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer of Comstock, and with me is Roland Burns, our President and Chief Financial Officer, Dan Harrison, our Chief Operating Officer, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations. Please refer to Slide 2 on our presentation and note that our discussion today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws. While we believe the expectations in such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. If you would turn to Slide 3.
You know, our corporate team of 255 strong want to thank you for joining the call today. We've been very active over the last 100 days, with all hands focused on continuing to batten down the hatches in order to manage our assets and continue to create value during this weak period for natural gas. Actions and achievements in the last 100 days have involved many of our stakeholders, including our bondholders, our bank group, our major stakeholder, Jerry Jones, and our service providers. On 15 March, we closed on an acquisition that enabled us to add 198,000 net acres to our Western Haynesville play, which were substantially held by production, so we do not have to increase our drilling activity in order to retain the acreage. In the quarter, we turned 4 new Western Haynesville wells to sales.
Each one looks fantastic. We're now drilling on two well pads, which will reduce our cost, and we recently also reduced our drilling days to 54. Dan Harrison will give a full report on our progress on the 450,000 net acre play later in the call. On 25 March, the Jones family purchased an additional $100.5 million of Comstock stock that demonstrated their confidence in our business plan, including the Western Haynesville acreage acquisition. On 2nd April, our bondholders stepped up in our $400 million new senior notes offering. The bonds were priced tighter to treasuries than any of our other bonds that we have issued since 1999. On 30th April, our bank lending group reaffirmed our borrowing base of $2 billion with a $1.5 billion commitment.
That has allowed us now to have $1.3 billion of liquidity. With the demand for natural gas growing in the future to service increased power generation, industrial, and LNG demand, as well as future demand to power AI, we're well-positioned to deliver clean, responsible produced natural gas from our 800,000 net acres in the Haynesville. We have over 30 years of drilling inventory, which we are adding to as we unlock value in our 450,000 net acres in the Western Haynesville one well at a time. I want to thank you for supporting your company, Comstock Resources. On Slide 3, we'll summarize the highlights of the Q1. The financial results continued to be heavily impacted by the continued weak natural gas prices.
Oil and gas sales, including hedging, were $336 million in the quarter, and we generated cash flow from operations of $182 million or $0.65 per share, and adjusted EBITDA was $230 million. Our adjusted net loss was $0.03 per share for the quarter. To strengthen our balance sheet, we added $100.5 million to our liquidity with a private placement of equity with our major stockholder, Jerry Jones. We continue to have strong results from our drilling program. In the first quarter, we drilled 16 successful operated Haynesville and Bossier shale horizontal wells in the quarter, with an average lateral length of 9,845 feet.
We turned to sales 18 successful operated Haynesville and Bossier shale horizontal wells with an average IP rate of 27 million cubic ft per day and an average lateral length of 9,227ft. We're continuing to progress in our Western Haynesville exploratory play. We added 198,000 net acres to our expansive Western Haynesville acreage position in Q1, increasing our total acreage position in the play to over 450,000 net acres. Since we last reported earnings, we have turned four additional wells to sales in the Western Haynesville and now have 12 successful wells in our new play. The Glass, Farley, Harrison, and Ingram Martin wells were all completed in the Haynesville shale, and each had IP rates of 35 to 38 million cubic feet per day.
We currently have two rigs running in the play, both of which are drilling on two well pads. We continue to lower our cost to drill these wells. In our last well, we were able to reduce the drilling days to 54 days. I'll now have Roland go over the Q1 financial results. Roland?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
All right. Thanks. Thanks, Jay. On Slide 4, we cover our Q1 financial results. Our production in the quarter of 1.5 BCFE per day increased 10% from Q1 2023. The low natural gas prices resulted in oil and gas sales in the quarter of $336 million, declining 14% from 2023's Q1 level, despite the 10% production increase. EBITDAX for the quarter was $230 million, and we generated $182 million of cash flow during Q1. We reported an adjusted net loss of $8.5 million for Q1, or $0.03 per share, as compared to income of $92 million in Q1 2023. Slide 5, we kind of break down our natural gas price realization in the quarter.
During Q1, the quarterly NYMEX settlement price averaged $2.24, which was $0.17 lower than the average Henry Hub spot price in the quarter of the daily prices of $2.41. Our realized gas price during Q1 averaged $2.06, reflecting an $0.18 differential to the settlement price and a $0.23 differential to our reference price. In Q1, we were 26% hedged, so this improved our realized price in Q1 to $2.40. In the volatile quarter, we also lost $800,000 on our third-party marketing activities. Slide 6, we update our hedge position.
Since we last reported, we've been very busy adding some hedges to kind of build out our hedge positions for next year in 2026, as well as improving the amount that we've hedged for Q4 of this year. We added 300 million a day of swaps covering the period of, I mean, October 2024 through December 2026 at an average price of $3.51 per Mcf. We added 75 million a day of swaps just for 2025 at an average swap price of $3.50. We added 150 million a day of collars in 2025 with a floor price of $3.50 and an average ceiling price of $3.80. We've also hedged some in 2026.
We have $250 million a day of collars that we added for 2026, which had a floor price of $3.50 and an average ceiling price of $3.98. As a result of this activity, we're almost 50% hedged for Q4 of this year, and we're about, you know, about 1/3 hedged for each of 2025 and 2026. We'll continue to look to opportunistically add to our hedged positions over time in order to get close to that 50% hedged kind of target that we have. We continue to put in positions that give us very meaningful floor protection. As you can see, that's kind of sitting around the $3.50 area.
On Slide 7, we detail our operating cost per Mcfe and our EBITDAX margin in Q1. Our operating cost for averaged to $0.76 per Mcfe produced, which was $0.05 lower than our Q4 rate. We saw some improvement in our production and ad valorem taxes, which were down 10%, but our other costs were up a little bit to slightly offset that. Our EBITDAX margin after hedging came in at 68% in Q1. That was a similar margin to the margin that we had in Q4, despite the fact that we had lower prices in Q1 of this year. On Slide 8, we recap our spending on drilling and other development activity.
You know, for the quarter, we spent a total of $256 million on our drilling activities, including $252 million that directly relates to the Haynesville and Bossier shale drilling program. We only spent $4 million on other development activity in the quarter. We drilled 16 or 14.3 net wells in our Haynesville program, and we turned 18 or 16.3 operated wells to sales in the quarter. These wells had an average IP rate of 27 million per day. In the quarter, we also did have four short lateral Bossier wells which were drilled, which probably dilute the numbers a little bit, but they were drilled to hold acreage. On Slide 9, we recap our balance sheet at the end of Q1.
We ended the quarter with $540 million in borrowings outstanding on our credit facility, giving us $2.7 billion in total debt, including our outstanding senior notes. As Jay referenced, on 25th March, we sold 12.5 million shares to our majority stockholder for $100.5 million in a private placement. The proceeds from that offering helped offset some of the cost of our Western Haynesville acreage acquisition program. Just after the end of Q1, we issued $400 million of additional senior notes due in 2029, and we used the proceeds to pay down the borrowings under our bank facility. The bond offering increased our liquidity on a pro forma basis to $1.3 billion.
Then lastly, on 30th April, our bank group reaffirmed our borrowing base at $2 billion, and our elected commitment of $1.5 billion kinda remained the same. I'll now turn the call over to Dan to discuss the operations in more detail.
Daniel Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Okay, thank you, Roland. Over on Slide 10, this is our current drilling inventory that we have, where we're at the end of Q1. Our total operated inventory currently has 1,702 gross locations, 1,296 net locations, which equates to a 76% average working interest across the operated inventory. On the non-operated inventory, we have 1,254 gross locations and 165 net locations, which represents a 13% average working interest on the non-operated inventory. The drilling inventory is split between Haynesville and Bossier locations. We have it split down into our four different groups.
Our short laterals are up to 5,000ft long, medium laterals at 5,000 to 8,500ft, long laterals at 8,500ft to 10,000ft, and then our extra-long laterals for everything over 10,000ft. If you look at each group in our gross operated inventory, we have 278 short laterals, 348 medium laterals, 433 long laterals, and 643 extra-long laterals. This gross operated inventory is evenly split with 51% in the Haynesville and 49% in the Bossier. 63% of our gross operated inventory has laterals longer than 8,500 feet, and 38% of our gross operated inventory, or the 643 locations, have lateral lengths surpassing 10,000ft.
The average lateral length in our inventory now stands at 9,015ft. This is up slightly from 8,971ft that we had at the end of Q4. Based on our near-term activity levels, this inventory provides us with over 30 years of future drilling locations. On Slide 11 is a chart outlining progress to date on our average lateral length drilled based on the wells that we have turned to sales. During Q1, we turned 18 wells to sales with an average lateral length of 9,229ft. The individual lengths range from 4,228ft up to 14,308ft. Our record longest laterals still stands at 15,726ft.
12 of the 18 wells we turned to sales during the quarter had laterals exceeding 8,500ft, including four with laterals longer than 13,500ft. As I mentioned, Roland mentioned earlier, our 9,229-foot average lateral length this quarter represents a departure from the upward trend we've been on for the last several years, and this is due to a handful of short laterals that were drilled on some isolated sections to preserve acreage while we're in this low gas price environment. We're not planning to drill any additional short lateral wells, and we do expect our average lateral length will exceed 10,000ft for the remaining wells that we turn to sales this year.
Included in our 18 wells turned to sales for the quarter are four wells that are located on our Western Haynesville acreage. These four wells had an average lateral length of 9,608ft. To recap our longer lateral wells, we have drilled 91 wells. To date, we've drilled 91 wells with laterals over 10,000ft, 33 wells with laterals over 14,000ft. On Slide 12, we recap our new well activity. Since we last provided our well results in mid-February, we have turned to sales and tested 14 new wells since our last conference call. This group of wells had individual IP rates ranging from 9 million up to 38 million cubic feet a day, with an average test rate of 25 million cubic feet a day.
The average lateral length was 8,031ft, with the individual laterals ran from 4,228ft up to 14,137ft. Since our last call, we have turned four additional wells to sales in the Western Haynesville. The Glass, the Farley, the Harrison, and the Ingram Martin wells achieved IP rates of 35 million to 38 million cubic ft a day, and all four of these wells targeted the Haynesville shale. Regarding our current activity levels, we are now running five rigs, and this is after we dropped two rigs during Q1, and we are running two full-time frac rigs. Two of these five rigs are currently drilling in the Western Haynesville, and both of these rigs are now drilling on the first of our two well pads, which will yield increased efficiencies.
Now that we have our two Western Haynesville rigs drilling on two well pads, we will not have any additional wells turned into sales in the Western Haynesville until early in Q4. Slide 13 summarizes our D&C costs through Q1 for our benchmark long lateral wells. This is the wells located on our legacy core East Texas and North Louisiana acreage. Our benchmark wells cover all laterals greater than 8,500ft long. During the quarter, we turned 14 wells to sales that were on our core acreage, and eight of these 14 wells fell into our benchmark long lateral group. In Q1, our D&C costs averaged $1,501 per foot on these benchmark wells, which reflects a 1% increase compared to Q4 of last year.
Our Q1 drilling cost averaged $714 a foot, which is a 17% increase compared to Q4. The higher drilling costs were primarily result of all eight of our benchmark long lateral wells during this quarter being concentrated in our higher drilling cost areas. Our Q1 completion cost came in at $787 a foot. This represents a 10% decrease compared to Q4. This mainly stems from the lower gas prices, which has led to the lower basin-wide completion activity and lower frac costs. As stated earlier, we did drop the two rigs during the Q1, and we are now running five rigs. Our current outlook has us holding steady at five rigs for the remainder of the year.
On the completion side, we are today running the two full-time frac crews, and we will stay at this level through the end of Q2. However, with the lower rig activity, we anticipate only working the equivalent of 1.5 frac crews during H2. On Slide 14, we highlight our continued improvement related to greenhouse gas and methane emissions. We reported a greenhouse gas intensity of 3.45kg CO2 equivalent per BOE of production. This is a 1% improvement versus 2022, increasing the improvement to 4% over the past two years. We reported a methane emission intensity of 0.04%, which is an 11% improvement versus 2022 and a 26% improvement over the past two years.
We achieved those emissions improvements despite our increased focus on the higher intensity Western Haynesville. In addition, our turn to sales lateral footage increased by 15% in 2023. COO, Comstock Resources
Can you ask that again?
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Sure. Of the 2024 operational plan, in Q1, there were four of those Bossier wells, shorter laterals required to hold the acreage. How much of that should we expect to be part of that?
Daniel Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
There's no more.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Daniel Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
I'll tell you. Interestingly enough, you know, we do have some additional sections that will come up. We're actually gonna drill one of these horseshoe wells, you know, later this year. I'll go ahead and kinda tell you that. That's kinda something that we're looking forward to trying. We don't have many of these isolated sections left where we'll have any of those issues.
Jay Allison
CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think the key to that is, if you don't think they're valuable, you don't drill them. We think they're valuable enough to drill them. Even if they're shorter, I mean, the-
Daniel Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Jay Allison
CEO, Comstock Resources
They're very economic.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
We're excited about the horseshoe design, and it could eliminate, you know, the stranded, you know, shorties, as we like to call them. You know, the 5,000ft lateral wells. It has the potential to allow you to eliminate those and turn it into a horseshoe well and have a long lateral well, you know, on one section. That's. That'll be kind of an exciting thing to do here later in the year.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks for the clarity.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Because we do believe that shorter laterals in the Western Haynesville are definitely our lowest return projects just because of the so much cost into the well and, you know, the reserves you recover with only that shorter lateral. The ability to eliminate a lot of those out of our inventory and turn them into long is, you know, it will be very enhancing.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Much appreciated.
Operator
Thank you. I'm showing no further questions at this time. I'd now like to turn it back to Jay Allison for closing remarks.
Jay Allison
CEO, Comstock Resources
Okay, perfect. Again, I know everybody's time is valuable, and we thank you for sharing your time with us. You know, Comstock, we do recognize the growing need for natural gas around the world. I mean, our long-term goal, as we've said over and over and over, is to be a significant supplier to the growing LNG market that's developing really several hundred miles from our Haynesville shale operations, including our Western Haynesville area. We're gonna be good stewards with your money. We wanna thank the bondholders. We wanna thank our banks that support us. We wanna thank the Joneses that support us and the other stakeholders, and the service companies. Everybody over the last 100 days has kinda teamed up and has helped Comstock. We're thankful for that. Thank you for your time.
Operator
Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This concludes the program. You may now disconnect.
